difficultyReason: Scientific argument that requires confirming an implicit assumption about measurement reliability. The correct answer rules out an alternative explanation (soil composition rather than rainfall) by confirming the experimental controls. Four distractors include a plausible irrelevant fact, an opposite-direction answer, a choice that strengthens a neighboring premise, and an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Researchers studying drought tolerance compared two strains of wheat grown in identical greenhouse conditions. Strain A consistently produced 30 percent more grain than Strain B when water was reduced to half the normal level. The researchers concluded that Strain A has superior drought tolerance.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strain A was developed in an arid region where low rainfall is common throughout the growing season.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under normal water conditions, Strain A and Strain B produce comparable grain yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The greenhouse soil used in the experiment was identical in nutrient composition for both strains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other drought-tolerant wheat strains have been developed over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Strain B is known to produce higher yields than Strain A in cold climates.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that Strain A is superior specifically under drought conditions. If Strain A also outperformed Strain B under normal water conditions, the 30-percent advantage might simply reflect Strain A's generally higher productivity rather than drought tolerance. Showing that yields are comparable under normal conditions isolates water reduction as the key variable, directly strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: This introduces an alternative explanation — Strain A may have been selectively bred for arid conditions for reasons unrelated to the mechanism tested, which is more of a background fact than a strengthener for the experimental conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. Ruling out the possibility that Strain A simply always outperforms Strain B isolates the reduced-water condition as the cause of the yield difference, strengthening the drought-tolerance conclusion.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant to the conclusion. The researchers already stated identical greenhouse conditions; this merely reiterates a control that does not directly bridge the premise-to-conclusion gap about drought tolerance.
explanations.D: An unwarranted comparison — the existence of other drought-tolerant strains is irrelevant to whether Strain A's advantage specifically reflects drought tolerance.
explanations.E: This introduces a tangential fact about cold-climate performance that does not speak to the drought-condition comparison at issue.

difficultyReason: Medical/pharmacological argument where the correct answer confirms the load-bearing mechanism linking drug uptake to cognitive outcome. Distractors include a choice that strengthens a side premise, a plausible irrelevancy, an opposite-direction trap, and a comparison that doesn't close the gap.
stimulus: A clinical trial found that patients who took a daily low-dose aspirin for two years showed significantly less cognitive decline than a control group that received a placebo. The trial's lead physician concluded that low-dose aspirin probably slows cognitive aging.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-dose aspirin has well-documented anti-inflammatory effects throughout the body, including in brain tissue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Participants in the aspirin group were, on average, two years younger than those in the placebo group at the start of the trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cognitive decline is one of the most common complaints among patients over the age of sixty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the placebo group reported higher-than-average levels of daily stress during the trial period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other anti-inflammatory drugs have been shown to slow cognitive decline in animal models.

explanations.correct: The argument needs a plausible mechanism connecting aspirin to slower cognitive aging. Confirming that aspirin reduces inflammation in brain tissue supplies the missing causal link — neuroinflammation is associated with cognitive decline — making the conclusion more likely to hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Confirming the biological mechanism (anti-inflammatory action in brain tissue) bridges the gap between taking aspirin and experiencing less cognitive decline.
explanations.B: This is actually a weakener disguised as context: if the aspirin group was younger at baseline, the observed difference in cognitive decline may reflect the age difference rather than aspirin's effect.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The prevalence of cognitive complaints among older patients does not make aspirin's causal role more likely.
explanations.D: This introduces an alternative explanation for the placebo group's decline (stress) rather than confirming the aspirin mechanism, and does not straightforwardly strengthen the causal claim.
explanations.E: An unwarranted comparison — animal-model results for different drugs do not confirm that aspirin works in humans through the same pathway.

difficultyReason: Economics argument about minimum-wage policy where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for the observed employment stability. Traps include a choice that only strengthens a background premise, a topically related but irrelevant fact, and an opposite-direction answer.
stimulus: After a coastal city raised its minimum wage by 15 percent, economists observed that restaurant employment in the city remained stable over the following year. They concluded that the wage increase did not cause significant job losses in the restaurant sector.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restaurant revenues in the city increased during the same year, driven by a spike in tourism.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighboring cities that did not raise their minimum wage saw restaurant employment decline slightly over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city's overall unemployment rate fell by one percentage point in the year following the wage increase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restaurant owners in the city reported that the wage increase was smaller than they had anticipated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low-wage workers generally spend a higher proportion of their income locally than higher-wage workers do.

explanations.correct: A rival explanation for stable employment is that broader economic trends would have kept restaurant employment stable regardless of the wage increase. Showing that cities without the wage increase actually saw employment decline rules out a favorable economic tide as the explanation, strengthening the conclusion that the wage increase itself did not cause job losses.
explanations.A: This introduces an alternative explanation — tourism may have bolstered employment independently of the wage effect — which actually undermines rather than strengthens the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct. A comparison group that declined without the wage increase rules out the possibility that employment stability was simply a regional trend, isolating the wage policy as consistent with stable employment.
explanations.C: Strengthens a related claim about overall employment but does not specifically address restaurant-sector job losses or rule out confounds in that sector.
explanations.D: Speaks to restaurant owners' expectations but does not directly confirm that the wage increase lacked negative employment effects.
explanations.E: Introduces a spending-multiplier argument that is tangential; it might explain why revenues held up but does not directly address employment stability.

difficultyReason: Legal/policy argument about eyewitness reliability where the correct answer confirms the load-bearing empirical premise. Traps include a choice that merely restates the conclusion, an irrelevant statistic, a comparison that doesn't close the gap, and an opposite-direction trap.
stimulus: Defense attorneys have argued that eyewitness testimony obtained more than 48 hours after an event is likely to be less accurate than testimony obtained within 24 hours. Memory researchers have documented that stress hormones released during a traumatic event interfere with long-term memory consolidation. Based on this, attorneys claim that delayed eyewitness accounts should be given less weight in criminal trials.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the attorneys' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In controlled laboratory studies, participants who recalled a stressful event 72 hours later made significantly more errors than those who recalled it within 12 hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Memory researchers disagree about the precise threshold at which stress-related memory interference becomes legally significant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eyewitnesses to non-traumatic events also show some decline in recall accuracy over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some criminal convictions have later been overturned based on DNA evidence that contradicted eyewitness testimony.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defense attorneys are more likely to challenge eyewitness testimony than prosecutors are.

explanations.correct: The attorneys' argument depends on the empirical claim that delayed testimony is less accurate. Controlled laboratory evidence directly confirming greater error rates in delayed recall bolsters this load-bearing premise, strengthening the conclusion that such testimony deserves less weight.
explanations.A: Correct. Empirical evidence that delayed recall of stressful events produces more errors directly confirms the factual foundation of the attorneys' argument.
explanations.B: Introduces researcher disagreement, which if anything introduces doubt about the premise rather than strengthening it.
explanations.C: Potentially weakens the argument's specificity: if all eyewitness accounts decay equally, the stress-hormone mechanism is not distinctively important for traumatic events.
explanations.D: Shows that eyewitness testimony can be wrong but does not establish that delayed testimony is specifically less reliable than prompt testimony.
explanations.E: Irrelevant to the accuracy of delayed testimony; it describes attorneys' behavior, not the validity of the underlying claim.

difficultyReason: Technology/policy argument where the correct answer closes an analogical gap between two contexts. Traps include an irrelevant comparison, a choice that strengthens a neighboring but non-essential premise, a plausible opposite-direction trap, and an unwarranted analogy.
stimulus: City planners in Westbrook are considering adopting a congestion-pricing scheme — charging drivers a fee to enter the downtown core during peak hours — to reduce traffic gridlock. A transportation consultant cited evidence that a similar scheme reduced peak-hour traffic by 20 percent in the city of Harwick. The consultant argued that a comparable reduction could be achieved in Westbrook.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the consultant's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Westbrook and Harwick have similar urban layouts, comparable public transit alternatives, and comparable proportions of commuters who drive to the downtown core.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing has been endorsed by several prominent urban planning organizations as an effective traffic-management tool.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Westbrook's downtown core currently experiences some of the worst traffic gridlock in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Harwick's congestion-pricing scheme was introduced during an economic downturn, when fewer commuters could afford the added cost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some Westbrook residents have already expressed support for measures that would reduce downtown traffic.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: what worked in Harwick will work in Westbrook. The critical gap is whether the two cities are similar enough for the result to transfer. Confirming that both cities share the key features — urban layout, transit alternatives, and commuter profile — that drive the effectiveness of congestion pricing closes this analogical gap directly.
explanations.A: Correct. Establishing that the two cities share the structural features relevant to congestion pricing makes the analogy more reliable and strengthens the prediction.
explanations.B: Provides endorsement from authorities but does not address whether Harwick's result is transferable to Westbrook specifically.
explanations.C: Confirms that the problem exists in Westbrook but says nothing about whether the Harwick solution would work there.
explanations.D: Actually weakens the analogy: if Harwick's success was partly due to economic conditions suppressing driving, the same success may not replicate in Westbrook under different economic conditions.
explanations.E: Resident support affects political feasibility, not whether the scheme would achieve a comparable traffic reduction.

difficultyReason: History/archaeology argument relying on an assumption about artifact preservation. The correct answer confirms the instrument-sensitivity premise — that the absence of evidence reflects actual absence rather than failed detection. Traps include a tangential archaeological fact, a choice that strengthens a neighboring premise, an irrelevant comparison, and a concealed weakener.
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a Bronze Age settlement found no iron tools in any of the site's seventeen distinct occupation layers. They concluded that the settlement's inhabitants almost certainly did not use iron tools during any phase of the settlement's occupation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron tools, if present and made of the alloys typical of that era, would have left detectable oxide traces in the soil even if the tools themselves had fully corroded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronze tools recovered from the site show wear patterns consistent with heavy agricultural use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron smelting was not widespread in the region until several centuries after the settlement was abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The settlement's seventeen occupation layers span approximately four hundred years of continuous habitation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Archaeologists at a nearby site of the same period found iron tools in only two of eleven occupation layers.

explanations.correct: The argument's weak point is the possibility that iron tools existed but left no physical trace — a classic 'absence of evidence' concern. Confirming that iron would have left detectable chemical residues even after corrosion means the absence of any such traces genuinely indicates the absence of iron use, directly strengthening the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Establishes that the excavation method would have detected iron even in degraded form, ruling out the alternative that iron tools existed but were simply undetectable.
explanations.B: Confirms heavy tool use of bronze but is irrelevant to whether iron was also present; it neither rules out nor confirms iron use.
explanations.C: Strengthens a background premise that iron was unavailable, but the argument concludes from archaeological evidence rather than from regional timing; this also makes the argument somewhat redundant rather than directly supporting the evidence-based inference.
explanations.D: Confirms the scope of the search but does not address whether the evidence would have survived if iron had been used.
explanations.E: An unwarranted comparison: the neighboring site's pattern does not directly bear on what the absence of iron at this site proves.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy argument about animal welfare labeling where the correct answer rules out an alternative explanation for consumer behavior change. Traps include an irrelevant statistic, a choice that only reaffirms a background fact, a comparison that misses the causal gap, and a subtle opposite-direction trap.
stimulus: After a national grocery chain began displaying animal welfare rating labels on meat products, sales of higher-rated products increased by 18 percent over six months while sales of lower-rated products declined. The chain's marketing director concluded that the labels caused consumers to shift their purchasing toward more humanely produced meat.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grocery chain did not change the prices of any of its meat products during the six-month period after the labels were introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer surveys conducted before the label rollout indicated that most shoppers claimed to care about animal welfare.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sales trends for non-meat products at the same chain remained flat during the six-month period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A prominent animal welfare documentary was released and widely viewed in the same six-month period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other grocery chains that did not use the rating labels saw no significant change in the ratio of higher- to lower-rated meat sales during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument claims the labels caused the purchasing shift. A rival explanation is that broader cultural trends — such as increased animal welfare awareness — drove the change regardless of the labels. Showing that chains without the labels saw no comparable shift rules out this industry-wide trend as an alternative cause, isolating the labels as the likely driver.
explanations.A: Rules out price changes as an explanation, which strengthens the argument somewhat, but does not address broader cultural or media-driven shifts in consumer attitudes that could explain the trend at this chain.
explanations.B: Pre-existing consumer attitudes are a background condition, not evidence that the labels caused the shift; consumers may have already favored higher-welfare products before the labels.
explanations.C: Flat non-meat sales show that the shift was specific to meat but do not address whether the labels rather than other factors caused it.
explanations.D: This introduces an alternative cause — a documentary may have shifted consumer preferences chain-wide, irrespective of the labels — and thus weakens rather than strengthens.
explanations.E: Correct. The absence of a comparable shift at chains lacking the labels rules out the alternative that industry-wide consumer trends drove the change, strengthening the causal role of the labels.

difficultyReason: Linguistics argument where the correct answer confirms the load-bearing mechanism about language acquisition. Traps include a choice that bolsters only a peripheral premise, an irrelevant comparison between unrelated languages, a plausible-sounding weakener, and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact.
stimulus: Children who grow up in bilingual households consistently acquire both languages to native proficiency without formal instruction. Linguists have argued that this is because children under age seven have a neurological window of heightened language plasticity during which any language they are regularly exposed to will be acquired naturally. Since children in bilingual households receive regular exposure to both languages, their native-level proficiency in both follows directly from this neurological mechanism.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults who attempt to learn a second language rarely achieve the same level of proficiency as those who acquired it in childhood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brain imaging studies show that children under age seven process newly heard language in regions associated with native-language acquisition, whereas older learners recruit different neural pathways.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual households exist in nearly every country and across a wide range of socioeconomic groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some children in bilingual households eventually become dominant in one language as adults, using the other language less frequently.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Children who learn sign language alongside a spoken language also achieve native proficiency in both before age seven.

explanations.correct: The argument's central premise is the neurological plasticity window. Brain imaging evidence directly confirming that young children use native-language acquisition circuits for new languages — while older learners use different circuits — bolsters the existence and importance of that window, strengthening the mechanistic claim that underlies the conclusion.
explanations.A: Consistent with the plasticity-window hypothesis and provides indirect support, but it addresses a separate contrast (child vs. adult) rather than directly confirming the neurological mechanism at work in children under seven.
explanations.B: Correct. Direct neuroimaging evidence for the distinct neural process in children under seven confirms the load-bearing mechanism the argument depends on.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant — the prevalence of bilingual households across demographics does not speak to the neurological mechanism.
explanations.D: This is a mild weakener: if children eventually become dominant in one language, it suggests the second language may not be maintained at full native proficiency, which complicates the conclusion.
explanations.E: Extends the plasticity-window claim to sign language, which is interesting but not directly relevant to the argument about bilingual spoken-language acquisition.

difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy argument about a river restoration project where the correct answer rules out a confounding variable. Traps include a choice that only confirms project implementation, an irrelevant generalization, an opposite-direction trap, and a comparison that addresses a neighboring conclusion rather than the core one.
stimulus: Following the removal of a hydroelectric dam on the Kelner River, native salmon populations in the river increased by 40 percent over three years. Environmental groups cited the dam removal as the cause of the salmon recovery and argued that removing dams is an effective restoration strategy.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Salmon populations in the Kelner River had been declining steadily for the twenty years the dam was in operation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ocean conditions in the three years following the dam removal were unusually favorable for Pacific salmon survival and growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salmon populations in comparable rivers where no dams were removed remained stable or declined slightly during the same three-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dam removal project also involved replanting native vegetation along the riverbanks, which provides shade and reduces water temperature.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dam removal projects are less expensive, on average, than dam retrofitting projects that attempt to add fish ladders.

explanations.correct: A key alternative explanation is that broader environmental factors — ocean conditions, precipitation cycles, or reduced fishing pressure — caused the salmon increase independently of the dam removal. Showing that comparable rivers without dam removal did not see similar increases rules out this region-wide trend, isolating the dam removal as the probable cause.
explanations.A: Confirms that the dam was associated with prior decline, which is consistent with the argument, but does not rule out the possibility that the post-removal increase was driven by other factors unrelated to the dam.
explanations.B: This is an opposite-direction trap — it introduces an alternative explanation (favorable ocean conditions) that weakens the causal attribution to dam removal.
explanations.C: Correct. Comparable rivers without dam removal not recovering rules out environmental trends as the explanation, directly strengthening the causal claim.
explanations.D: This introduces an alternative mechanism (bank revegetation) that could explain the salmon increase independent of dam removal, which weakens rather than strengthens the specific causal attribution.
explanations.E: Addresses cost-effectiveness, which is relevant to policy advocacy but irrelevant to whether dam removal actually caused the salmon increase.

difficultyReason: Arts/cultural policy argument where the correct answer confirms a load-bearing empirical assumption about audience behavior. Traps include a choice that only restates a premise differently, an irrelevant institutional comparison, an opposite-direction trap about funding, and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact about artistic quality.
stimulus: A municipal arts council argued that subsidizing free public concerts in city parks increases long-term attendance at the city's paid performing arts venues. The council's reasoning was that residents who attend free outdoor concerts develop an appreciation for live performance that motivates them to subsequently purchase tickets to indoor events.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the arts council's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In cities with established free outdoor concert programs, surveys show that a majority of regular ticketholders at paid indoor venues attended free outdoor performances before becoming paying patrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cost of subsidizing free outdoor concerts is substantially lower than the cost of advertising campaigns aimed at attracting new audiences to paid venues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some residents who attend free outdoor concerts later report that they preferred the outdoor experience and chose not to purchase indoor venue tickets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Municipal arts councils in other regions have successfully increased arts funding by demonstrating broad community engagement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The performing arts venues in the city regularly present performances by nationally recognized artists.

explanations.correct: The argument depends on the claim that free outdoor concerts serve as a gateway to paid indoor attendance. Survey data showing that most regular ticketholders at paid venues first attended free outdoor concerts directly confirms this pathway, providing strong support for the council's causal reasoning.
explanations.A: Correct. Evidence that a majority of paying indoor patrons first attended free outdoor events confirms the gateway mechanism the argument relies on.
explanations.B: Addresses cost efficiency relative to advertising, which is relevant to budget decisions but does not support the claim that free concerts actually convert attendees into paying patrons.
explanations.C: This is an opposite-direction trap — it highlights a scenario where the mechanism fails (free-concert attendees prefer outdoor and don't purchase indoor tickets), weakening rather than strengthening.
explanations.D: An unwarranted comparison: other councils' funding success through engagement metrics does not confirm that the gateway mechanism operates in this city.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant — the caliber of indoor performances does not address whether free outdoor concerts motivate residents to attend those performances.
